title: Developing and Maintaining an Open-Source Repository of AI Evaluations: Challenges and Insights (plus Inspect Evals docs/methodology.md "Benchmark Implementation Methodology")
date: Paper: 2025-07-09 (arXiv v1; the only version as of 2026-10-11). methodology.md: first commit 2025-07-14 (9184ab85), last modified 2026-07-02 (be78f6c1); read the current version and the 2025-07-14 original.
authors: Alexandra Abbas, Celia Waggoner, Justin Olive (Arcadia Impact, London); methodology.md: UK AISI / inspect_evals maintainers and contributors
venue: arXiv preprint (cs.CL), ICML-style template with Impact Statement; no published venue found. OpenAlex (W4416104403) lists arXiv only and 0 citing works as of 2026-10-11. Citation count not checked on Semantic Scholar.
what_it_does: A 6-page experience report on eight months of maintaining inspect_evals (70+ community-ported evaluations). The port-validation content is one paragraph (Sec. 3.3.1 "Result validation"): frontier models are run on evaluation subsets and results must match reference implementations "within +/-5% deviation"; deviations are investigated manually and are "fairly common" because papers omit temperature/endpoint details. Sec. 3.4 says contributors usually validate on random subsets (max $100 or 10-20% of data), admits "This approach introduces noise", and says Q&A evals "may be run multiple times" to get CIs and "test whether performance differences exceed random variation" (a difference test, not equivalence; no numbers shown). Sec. 3.5 applies Miller (2024)'s rule E[sigma_i^2]/K << Var(x-bar) to pick epoch counts. Sec. 3.6.2 gives unpaired and paired (per-question difference) 95% CIs for comparing two models on the same eval, and criticises mean-only leaderboards. Harbor, parity experiments, range overlap, TOST and equivalence margins are never mentioned. There is no table or analysis of how ports compared with originals across the repository. The current methodology.md contains no numeric tolerance at all: it says "Run against known reference implementations", "Document acceptable discrepancies (e.g. minor differences due to prompt formatting or randomization)" and "perform repeated runs or paired comparisons across models to estimate uncertainty". The current tooling (tools/evaluation_report.py, eval-report-workflow skill) emits a Reference/delta/stderr column with no threshold or test; the Generality Labs template says only that the implementation "needs to be compared against the original paper or an existing reputable leaderboard result". Agent-written validity reports (e.g. agent_artefacts/macbench_1_A, 2026-04-24) report a point gap in percentage points and note aggregate artifacts are "weaker evidence for exact sample-by-sample parity". The validation target is usually published paper numbers, not a same-agent head-to-head run of the original harness; only the SWE-bench README recommends re-scoring Inspect outputs with the original harness. Inspect's Harbor link is an integration package (inspect_harbor), not a parity analysis.
what_it_leaves_open: Everything our paper plans: (1) no analysis of Harbor's parity_experiment.json data or any port-vs-original dataset; (2) no critique of a matching criterion (its own +/-5% is asserted without justification: on a 100-sample subset at ~50% accuracy, SE is ~5 points, so the tolerance is roughly +/-1 SE and would pass large true gaps; it never states a false-alarm or miss rate); (3) no equivalence test or TOST, no stated equivalence margin, no derivation of runs/samples needed to establish equivalence within a margin; (4) no paired per-task analysis between a port and the original (paired analysis is used only between two models on one eval); (5) no systematic study of whether the 70+ ports match their originals, only the remark that deviations are "fairly common"; (6) its Sec. 4 explicitly lists "Automated validation of evaluation implementations" and "Cost-efficient evaluation sampling strategies" for validation as open future work. Our paper can position its TOST margin and run-count protocol against Inspect's informal fixed +/-5% tolerance on subsets (and against Harbor's range-overlap / SEM rule), and can reuse Inspect's paired-difference CI machinery (Sec. 3.6.2, Miller 2024) by applying it to per-task original-vs-port pairs instead of model-vs-model pairs.

title: Every Eval Ever: A Unifying Schema and Community Repository for AI Evaluation Results
date: 2026-06-12 (arXiv v1; only version as of 2026-10-11)
authors: Jan Batzner, Sree Harsha Nelaturu, Damian Stachura, Anastassia Kornilova (lead authors); Jon Crall, Tommaso Cerruti, Yanan Long, Yifan Mai, Sanchit Ahuja, Asaf Yehudai, Marek Suppa, John P. Lalor, Oluwagbemike Olowe (top contributors); 27 further contributors; advisors Stella Biderman, Irene Solaiman, Zeerak Talat, Anka Reuel, Mubashara Akhtar, Gjergji Kasneci, Avijit Ghosh, Leshem Choshen (48 authors total; EvalEval Coalition)
venue: arXiv preprint 2606.14516 [cs.AI, cs.CL, cs.CY]; no venue or comments field on the abs page; code cited as "Anonymous Github" so apparently under anonymous review
what_it_does: Proposes a shared JSON schema (aggregate + instance-level) for AI evaluation results, converters from HELM / lm-eval-harness / Inspect AI and ~15 leaderboards, a validation pipeline, and a crowdsourced Hugging Face datastore (22,235 models, 2,273 benchmarks, 31 formats). Four case studies: (1) cost-accuracy tradeoffs in agentic evals (CocoaBench, HAL CORE-Bench); (2) perplexity normalization mismatches (GPTQ script vs vLLM+lm-eval); (3) 'reproducibility gaps': the authors re-ran 3 models (Pythia-6.9B, Vicuna-7B v1.3, Falcon-7B) on 14 single-turn HELM scenarios with the same HELM recipe, converted official HELM records and local re-runs to EEE, aligned instances by a SHA-256 sample_hash of prompt+reference, and reported per cell the percentage of aligned (instance, core metric) score pairs identical up to 1e-9 tolerance (39/42 cells joined; Entity-Matching failed to join because a pandas row-order change selected different Abt-Buy examples; SyntheticReasoning-Natural official Pythia completions were empty due to a stop-sequence/Together.ai serving artifact; WikiFact ~92% agreement explained by an independent-Bernoulli model of stochastic temperature=1.0 decoding, E[p^2+(1-p)^2]+2Var(p)); (4) IRT meta-analysis on GPQA Diamond, Wordle Arena, JudgeBench. Harbor appears only as reference [38] in a Related Work list ('made first steps towards achieving it [8, 49, 64, 38, 96]'); 'parity' appears zero times in HTML and PDF; 'overlap' appears only as 'content-hash overlap' (sample joins); 'TOST', hypothesis test, p-value, CI never appear in any analysis; the single 'equivalence' mention (Limitations) is about record deduplication criteria. Terminal-Bench 2.0 appears only as a leaderboard converter that 'preserves the leaderboard's accuracy and standard-error values'. EEE GitHub org check: 'harbor' hits are Terminal-Bench leaderboard scrapers; 'parity'/'equivalence test' hits are build-parity scripts in eval-cards/auto-benchmarkcard, unrelated. Read depth: full HTML text plus Appendix F.3 recovered from the PDF (the arXiv HTML renders F.3 as an empty heading).
what_it_leaves_open: Everything in our contributions (1) and (2): it never looks at Harbor, adapters, parity experiments, parity_experiment.json, the HF parity dataset, or any acceptance rule for ports; it does not analyse the range-overlap criterion, false-alarm/miss rates, or k-dependence; it applies no inferential statistics at all (no CIs, no TOST, no margin, no pass/fail rule) to its official-vs-local comparison; its object is a same-harness reproduction of deterministic-mostly single-turn HELM scenarios on 7B models, not a cross-harness port of an agentic benchmark with k=3 noisy runs per side. What it does establish, and what we must position against for contribution (3): a systematic (3 models x 14 scenarios) per-instance, content-hash-aligned official-vs-reproduction agreement audit with root-cause forensics (example-set drift, serving artifacts, stochastic decoding), plus a probabilistic model of expected per-instance agreement under stochastic sampling. Our paired per-task analysis of Harbor parity data should cite this as the closest prior 'instance-level reproducibility audit', state that it is descriptive (agreement %) rather than inferential (equivalence within a margin), and that it concerns reproductions within one harness rather than ports between harnesses. It also motivates us: its abstract asserts frameworks 'produce divergent scores for nominally identical evaluations' without offering a decision rule for when two results count as the same benchmark, which is exactly the gap our equivalence-test protocol fills. The EEE datastore's terminal_bench_2 adapter (accuracy + SE per agent-model pair) is a potential data source but not an analysis.

title: Harbor Adapters and Harbor-Index: Infrastructure and a Curated Meta-Dataset for Large-Scale Agentic Evaluation
authors: Lin Shi, Haowei Lin, Zixuan Zhu, Xiaoyue Zhou, Xiang Li, Xiangning Lin, Yaxuan Deng, Han Xu, Yuangang Li, Shanda Li, Zizhao Chen, Hanwen Xing, ... (approx. 130 authors incl. Andy Konwinski, Nicholas Carlini, Sanmi Koyejo, Mike Merrill, Ludwig Schmidt, Alex Shaw); correspondence ls2282@cornell.edu, linhaowei@pku.edu.cn
what_it_does: The maintainers' paper. It publishes the parity data and states a criterion, but does not analyse the criterion or the data. Specifically: (a) Sec 2 and App D.4.2 describe the protocol: same agent/model/config on original and Harbor side, each side run k times (k=3 default), report mean ± sample SEM (s/sqrt(k)); pass rule stated as "means agree within a margin consistent with their standard errors" (D.4.2) and, in different words, "statistical equivalence with the original benchmark within sample SEM" (D.7 'Standards we enforce'). No margin is pre-specified, no test statistic, no CI, no power/false-alarm discussion anywhere (0 hits for TOST, confidence interval, null hypothesis, Type I/II, false positive rate; 'overlap' appears 6x, never about parity). (b) Tables 3-4 (App D.5) list ~57 adapters with Orig. vs Harbor pass rate as mean±SEM; parsing the HTML rows gives k=3 for 41 rows, k=1-2 for 7, up to k=8; 7 rows have SEM 0.0 on a side; no pass/fail or test column; one row (FrontierCS 68.9±11.5 vs 53.4±9.9, k=3) has a 15-point gap that still 'passes' because SEMs are huge. (c) App D.6 per-benchmark notes judge parity qualitatively ('residual disagreements reflect stochastic lv1 variation', 'aligned within seed variance'); exactly two benchmarks get a one-off difference test: SciCode 'sub-step accuracy aligned within a Welch t-test', DA-Code 'a permutation test shows no statistically significant difference'. Several adapters establish parity 'transitively' via a Terminal-Bench adapter with k=1 or 2 on a leg (Aider Polyglot, LiveCodeBench, QuixBugs, AlgoTune, ReplicationBench, SLDBench, CodePDE, SWE-smith). (d) parity_experiment.json is mentioned once (D.7); the HF dataset harborframework/parity-experiments is not mentioned (only kendx/Harbor-Adapter trajectories, E.1). (e) Miller 2024 'Adding error bars to evals' [105] is cited only for micro-benchmark uncertainty (Sec 5, App C), not applied to parity. (f) The repo guide adapters/ADAPTER_CONTRIBUTING.md (last touched 2026-09-23) says 'The two sides match if and only if their run-score ranges overlap' (line 331) and 'Close means with non-overlapping ranges do not constitute a match' (line 337); the paper never states or reconciles this range rule. The rest of the paper (large-scale eval of 16 model-harness configs on 54 benchmarks, PCA/LMM analyses, failure-mode taxonomy, Harbor-Index curation) is unrelated to parity. Coverage: all prose sections read (abstract, Sec 1-6, App C, D.1-D.7, E.1/E.3/E.4, I, J, Table 3-4 captions); tabular appendices (D.5 rows, E.2, E.5, G.2.2), App F/H and references were parsed or keyword-searched rather than read line by line.
what_it_leaves_open: Everything in our three planned contributions: (1) no error-rate analysis of any matching rule (neither the paper's SEM-margin wording nor the repo's range-overlap rule): no false-alarm or miss rates, nothing on behaviour as k grows, nothing on the rule rewarding noisy ports (the FrontierCS row is a ready example); (2) no re-analysis of Tables 3-4 with CIs or equivalence tests: with k=3 and SEMs of 1-3 points, 95% t-intervals on the difference span roughly ±4-13 points, which the paper never computes; (3) no protocol with a pre-specified margin, required run count, or paired per-task analysis (the contributor guide's debug playbook step 3 mentions listing tasks resolved on A-only/B-only as a heuristic, so our paired analysis should be framed as formalizing that). Also open: the discrepancy between the paper's 'statistical equivalence within sample SEM' claim and the repo's range-overlap implementation, and the burden-of-proof inversion in the two cases where a difference test (Welch t, permutation) is used as evidence of parity. App I lists 'improving adapter verification' as future work. Positioning caveats for our paper: we cannot say 'Harbor uses range overlap' without noting the paper itself states an SEM-based criterion; and we cannot say 'no statistical test is ever used' because two adapters use difference tests.

title: Shachi: A Modular, Controllable Framework for LLM-Based Agent-Based Modeling of Emergent Collective Behavior
date: v1 2025-09-26; v2 2025-10-10; v3 2026-06-15 (the TOST/equivalence section exists only in v3; v1 and v2 contain zero mentions of TOST or equivalence). Accepted to ALIFE 2026.
authors: So Kuroki, Yingtao Tian, Kou Misaki, Takashi Ikegami, Takuya Akiba, Yujin Tang (Sakana AI)
what_it_does: Shachi is an LLM agent-based-modeling (ABM) framework from Sakana AI that re-implements ("ports") ten prior LLM-ABM tasks (PsychoBench, CoMPosT, CognitiveBiases, EmotionBench, EmergentAnalogies, EconAgent, StockAgent, AuctionArena, Sotopia, OASIS) behind a unified Gym-style agent/environment interface. Its "Foundational Validation" (Sec 4.1) has two parts relevant to us. (a) Table 1 reports mean absolute error between the Shachi port and the original results for 8 tasks, compared only against a "naive random selection" or module-ablation baseline (App. B), i.e. a weak comparator that does not establish equivalence. (b) New in v3 (June 2026): Sec 4.1 + App. C.1 "Statistical Validation of Reproducibility" apply Two One-Sided Tests (TOST) to 3 of the 8 ports (EmergentAnalogies, AuctionArena, Sotopia; one per complexity level), N=30 samples per condition, 90% CI (alpha=0.05 per one-sided test), with pre-specified task-specific margins (Delta=0.05 accuracy, Delta=2.0 TrueSkill mu, Delta=0.20 Sotopia reward). Table 7 gives original-vs-Shachi mean +/- std, the 90% CI of the difference, and p(TOST) for 13 metrics; all pass. They explicitly justify testing only 3 tasks because TOST "require[s] a large sample size (N=30) per condition, which is computationally prohibitive". Zero mentions of Harbor, Terminal-Bench, parity experiments, parity_experiment.json, range overlap, or any adapter-contribution rule (full-text search: Harbor 0, parity 0, overlap 0). The accompanying repo SakanaAI/shachi has no TOST/equivalence code (the single code-search hit is the substring in ET.tostring).
what_it_leaves_open: Everything in our contributions (1) and (2) and most of (3). It never looks at Harbor or any agent-benchmark harness, never analyses parity_experiment.json or the HF parity dataset, and never discusses, critiques, or even names a range-overlap / SEM-overlap acceptance rule; it has no false-alarm/miss-rate analysis of any matching criterion, no analysis of the k=3 regime, no power or runs-needed calculation, and no paired per-task analysis (its tests are on aggregate scores). Its TOST margins are set ad hoc "based on the characteristics of each evaluation metric" with no justification or sensitivity analysis; "N=30 samples" is not defined (runs vs. items), and the "original" side appears to be the authors' own re-run of original code with different backend models than Table 1 (e.g. Gemini-2.5-flash-lite for AuctionArena, GPT-4o-mini for Sotopia) rather than the originally published numbers, so it is a self-run A/B, not a check against published results. Only 3 of 8 ports get a formal test; the other 5 rest on MAE vs. a random baseline. Domain is LLM-ABM simulations (ALIFE venue), not agentic coding/terminal benchmarks. What it does establish that we must cite and position against: a published precedent (June 2026) of using TOST with pre-stated margins, N=30 and 90% CIs to certify that a re-implemented benchmark task is equivalent to the original, plus an explicit cost argument that equivalence testing is too expensive to run on every port, which is exactly the tension our protocol (margin, runs needed, paired per-task reuse of existing per-task results) is designed to resolve.

title: UniACE: A Unified Framework for Evaluating LLM Agentic Capabilities
authors: Pengyu Zhu, Lijun Li, Yaxing Lyu, Qianxin Luo, Jingyi Yang, Yi Liu, Tingfeng Hui, Xinyu Yuan, Li Sun, Sen Su, Jing Shao (BUPT; Shanghai AI Lab; CQUPT; NCEPU)
venue: arXiv preprint, cs.AI (no venue or comments field on the abs page)
what_it_does: Builds UniACE, a single model-centric harness (instruction-tool-environment triplets, isolated per-task runtimes, optional offline snapshots, unified efficiency metrics and failure taxonomy) and migrates 7 agent benchmarks (AgentBench, BFCL, tau-bench, tau2-bench, BrowseComp, MultiAgentBench, Agent-SafetyBench; 24 domains) into it, then runs 15 models (400K rollouts). Sec. 4.2 / Table 1, Sec. 4.3 / Table 2 and Sec. 4.6 / Fig. 3 compare UniACE scores against "benchmark-reported scores (Orig.) obtained under their original frameworks" (Table 1 caption: "using the respective LLMs in their original evaluations"), i.e. a point comparison of one temperature-0 UniACE run per configuration against the number the benchmark's own harness reported. It finds "large bidirectional score changes and model-ranking reversals" (e.g. GPT-3.5-Turbo +26.6 on AgentBench DB; DeepSeek-V3.2 -23.8/-35.5/-11.1 on tau2-bench; tau-bench Retail ordering GPT-4o 61.2 > GPT-3.5 20.0 reverses to 55.7 < 28.7) and treats these as evidence of harness sensitivity, not as port-validation failures. Migration fidelity is argued by construction and manual inspection (App. H: "we manually verified that the migrated artefacts preserve the logic of the original release on a per-task basis"). App. E.1 is a one-task qualitative trace comparison (BFCL task #61, gemini-2.5-flash, original BFCL harness vs UniACE, same live web and tools), explicitly "diagnostic rather than causal". Harbor appears only as a related framework: Sec. 1 "Harbor primarily provides execution and mediation infrastructure", Sec. 2 "Harbor provides containerized infrastructure for executing and optimizing CLI-based agents", and a feature check-mark row in Table 4 (App. A), citing github.com/laude-institute/terminal-bench. No mention of adapters, parity experiments, parity_experiment.json, or any matching criterion. Whole-document keyword search: 0 hits for parity, TOST, confidence interval, standard error/deviation, p-value, seed, trial, pass@k, error bar; the hits for "overlap", "equivalent", "significant", "bootstrap", "margin" are all non-statistical. The only variance control is Sec. 4.1 "temperature set to 0 to reduce decoding variability"; no repeated runs, no uncertainty on any number. Appendix F (Cohen's kappa of LLM judge vs human on 300 samples) is the only statistic in the paper.
what_it_leaves_open: Everything in our core: (1) it never states or tests a criterion for when a re-implementation "matches" the original, so it cannot say whether a 2-point or 20-point difference is harness effect or run-to-run noise; (2) single runs per configuration mean the "Orig. vs Ours" gaps carry no uncertainty and the ranking-reversal claim is untested for significance; (3) no per-task paired comparison against the original harness even though it retains per-task execution records; (4) no equivalence margin, no TOST, no CI, no power/sample-size reasoning; (5) no engagement with Harbor's adapter/parity protocol or data, and no critique of range overlap. Its stance is the opposite of a parity check: divergence is reported as a feature ("These findings motivate reporting agent benchmark outcomes as properties of an explicit evaluation configuration"), whereas Harbor asserts its ports are the same benchmark. For us it is strong motivational evidence that ports can diverge by tens of points and flip rankings, and a positioning target ("a large systematic re-implementation study exists but with point estimates only"), not a competitor on the statistical question. Caveat on read depth: main text and Appendices A, E, F, H read; B, C, D, G, I (schemas, failure taxonomy, prompts) covered only by keyword search.

title: Adapters (Agent Guide) / Adapters (Human Guide) -- Harbor adapter contributing guide, Step 5 "Run Parity Experiments": "Matching criterion" and "Reporting format: mean ± sample SEM"
date: Range-overlap "Matching criterion" first appeared 2026-04-19 (commit 9ad34d5f, PR #1403 merged 2026-04-19T04:50Z) in docs/content/docs/datasets/adapters.mdx; "Reporting format: mean ± sample SEM" added 2026-04-22 (commit 6ecf6a31, PR #1496); file renamed to adapters/ADAPTER_CONTRIBUTING.md 2026-09-23 (commit 5f082d63, PR #3354). Current blob sha 1c6dd2b0, 63688 bytes, retrieved 2026-10-11.
authors: Harbor maintainers (harbor-framework). Matching-criterion text authored by Crystal Zhou (crystalxyz) in PR #1403; SEM reporting section by Crystal Zhou in PR #1496; file relocated by Kobe Chen in PR #3354. Adapter program contact named in the doc: Lin Shi (Cornell).
what_it_does: It is the maintainers' normative contributor spec (two concatenated docs: an "Agent Guide" of ~820 lines and a shorter "Human Guide"), not an analysis. Step 5 defines parity ("scores on both sides should be statistically indistinguishable"), then prescribes the acceptance test as pure range overlap: "The two sides match if and only if their run-score ranges overlap: max(side_A_runs) >= min(side_B_runs) AND max(side_B_runs) >= min(side_A_runs)". It explicitly rejects mean-based judgement ("Close means with non-overlapping ranges do not constitute a match") and puts the burden on non-overlap ("Non-overlap should be treated as a systematic adaptation error until evidence indicates otherwise"). The SEM section mandates mean ± sample SEM with the formula sqrt(sum((xi-xbar)^2)/(n(n-1))), requires n >= 2 ("3+ preferred"), and justifies SEM informally because it "shrinks as runs are added". The required execution order is sanity 5-10 tasks -> 1 full run -> 3 runs per side. Per-task analysis appears only in the "Debug playbook" step 3, triggered when overlap fails: "Per-task resolution on each side; list tasks resolved on A-only and on B-only. A roughly symmetric split suggests sampling noise"; step 5 suggests re-running high-variance tasks 5-10 times. Step 6 "complete when ... the run-score ranges overlap per the matching criterion". The same rule is operationalised in Harbor's LLM review bot (src/harbor/cli/adapter_review.py line 511, added in PR #1496): "'Within sample SEM' alone is neither necessary nor sufficient -- the required check is range overlap on original_runs vs harbor_runs". No simulation, no false-alarm/miss rates, no power or sample-size reasoning, no CI, no TOST or any hypothesis test, no margin, and no re-analysis of any parity_experiment.json data anywhere in the file. Note the candidate record's date is slightly off: the overlap rule came in via PR #1403 (2026-04-19), and PR #1496 (2026-04-22) only added the SEM section and the bot checklist line.
what_it_leaves_open: Everything our paper plans. (1) It never evaluates the operating characteristics of the overlap rule: no false-alarm rate at k=3, no miss rate for a fixed true gap, no observation that the rule gets more lenient as runs are added or that noisier ports pass more easily; it asserts the rule as an "if and only if" without justification. (2) It gives no equivalence margin, no CI, no TOST, and no way to say what "statistically indistinguishable" means operationally; the only statistic is SEM, and its own review-bot text concedes "within SEM" is "neither necessary nor sufficient", which conflicts with the Harbor paper's App. D wording "statistical equivalence ... within sample SEM" (arXiv 2609.04298 v3, App. D.7) -- a discrepancy our paper can document. (3) It never re-analyses the published parity_experiment.json / HF parity-experiments data; the per-task overlap analysis exists only as an informal debugging heuristic ("roughly symmetric split suggests sampling noise") with no test, no pairing, and no use for acceptance, so a formal paired per-task protocol with stated margin and run counts is untouched. Separately, the Harbor paper's per-adapter summaries mention ad hoc stats for a few adapters (a Welch t-test for SciCode, a permutation test for one data-science adapter; App. D.6, SciCode and DA-Code entries) but the guide itself prescribes none of these.

title: AgentCompass: A Unified Evaluation Infrastructure for Agent Capabilities
authors: AgentCompass Team, Shanghai AI Laboratory (23 authors, alphabetical: Kai Chen, Zichen Ding, Jiaye Ge, Shufan Jiang, Mo Li, Qingqiu Li, Zehao Li, Zonglin Li, Tianhao Liang, Shudong Liu, Zerun Ma, Zixin Shang, Wenhui Tian, Zun Wang, Liwei Wu, Zhenyu Wu, Jun Xu, Bowen Yang, Dingbo Yuan, Qi Zhang, Songyang Zhang, Peiheng Zhou, Dongsheng Zhu; corresponding: Zhu, Ma, Zhang)
venue: arXiv preprint (cs.AI, cs.SE). The GitHub repo description (open-compass/AgentCompass, seen 2026-10-11) tags it "[EMNLP 2026]"; the arXiv page itself shows no journal reference.
what_it_does: Systems paper (about 7,000 words, read in full from the arXiv HTML) introducing AgentCompass, an open-source agent-evaluation framework from Shanghai AI Lab that decouples Benchmark / Harness / Environment and natively ports 20+ benchmarks (tau-bench family, BrowseComp, GAIA, HLE, SciCode, SWE-bench Pro/Multilingual, Terminal-bench 2.x, SkillsBench, PinchBench, GDPVal-AC, ...). Harbor is cited exactly once, as a competing framework in Related Work. The only fidelity-related evidence is Table 3: 7 models on 8 benchmarks, each score "averaged over three independent runs", annotated with colored point deltas against the "closest available external reference" (model tech report or benchmark leaderboard; when both exist they take whichever is closer to their own number, App. A.2). Deltas run from -15.0 to +15.0 points; Sec. 4.2 attributes them to harness choice, harness version and ad-hoc adaptations and uses them to argue for a unified framework, not to test whether a port is faithful. No SEM, CI, error bars, significance test or equivalence test appears anywhere; the words parity, overlap, TOST and equivalence (in the statistical sense) do not occur; parity_experiment.json and Harbor's parity experiments are never mentioned. The rest of the paper is architecture (RunRequest, registries, asyncio runtime), trajectory analyzers, a reward-hacking count on SWE-Pro/Multilingual, and token-length plots. Separately, the repo's developer docs (docs/en/developer_guide/extensions/benchmark/validation_and_alignment.mdx, last commit bf4e9f94 on 2026-09-01, not in the paper) define an "Alignment Report" for new benchmark ports: run the full official split with k=1, report official score "and interval", run count, absolute delta, whether the comparison is "point-to-point or single-run-to-distribution", and an Aligned / Explained-difference / Not-aligned verdict, but with no numeric margin, no statistical test and no stated decision rule.
what_it_leaves_open: Everything our paper plans. It never asks whether a port reproduces the original benchmark: it reports a single point delta against a hand-picked reference with no uncertainty on either side, no margin, no run count for the official side and no equivalence logic, and its rule of choosing the closest official number when two exist biases deltas toward zero. It does not touch Harbor's parity data, the range-overlap rule, TOST, power at k=3, or a paired per-task analysis. For us it is a contrast case rather than a threat: a second large port collection (20+ benchmarks, EMNLP-tagged) whose fidelity check is even less formal than Harbor's overlap rule, which directly supports the motivation that nobody can currently tell whether a ported benchmark is still the same benchmark. Its developer docs' request for "official score and interval" and "point-to-point or single-run-to-distribution" shows the maintainers sense the problem but have no protocol, which is exactly the gap our equivalence-test protocol (stated margin, runs needed, paired per-task test) would fill. Worth one or two sentences in related work / motivation, possibly a footnote noting the closest-reference selection rule.

title: Beyond Metrics: A Critical Analysis of the Variability in Large Language Model Evaluation Frameworks
date: 2024-07-29 (v1 only; no later versions as of 2026-10-11)
authors: Marco AF Pimentel, Clément Christophe, Tathagata Raha, Prateek Munjal, Praveen K Kanithi, Shadab Khan (M42, Abu Dhabi)
venue: arXiv preprint (cs.AI, cs.CL), 15 pages; no journal reference or DOI on the abs page; OpenAlex lists it as a preprint with 0 citations
what_it_does: Read in full (8.3k words; Intro, Background, Methods, Results, Discussion, Appendices A-B). It is a 2024 cross-framework discrepancy study for multiple-choice QA, predating Harbor entirely. The authors describe how OpenCompass, EleutherAI lm-eval-harness and HELM score MCQs (next-token letter probability vs full-sequence log-likelihood vs generated-text exact match), then run Llama2-7B/13B/70B and Mistral-7B zero-shot on HellaSwag, MedQA, MMLU and OpenBookQA under four scoring rules (OpenCompass accuracy, raw loglik, token-normalised, byte-normalised; Sec 3.3, Table 2). The finding is that the same model on the same dataset moves by 5-26 accuracy points depending on the scoring rule (Sec 4-5), e.g. Llama2-70B on HellaSwag 64.8% to 83.8%. They then use Bland-Altman plots of correct-vs-wrong option length (Figs 2-3) to argue length normalisation reduces bias on HellaSwag but introduces it on MedQA. Every number is a single deterministic zero-shot run; there are no repeated runs, no confidence intervals, no standard errors, no hypothesis or equivalence test, no notion of an 'original' reference implementation that a re-implementation must match, and no criterion for when two implementations agree. The Bland-Altman plots (a method-agreement tool) are applied only to answer-option lengths, not to framework-vs-framework scores. A search of the full text finds zero occurrences of harbor, parity, equivalence, TOST, overlap, confidence interval, standard error, bootstrap, error bar, repeat, or seed.
what_it_leaves_open: Everything our paper plans. It does not touch Harbor or any adapter/port parity data; it does not define or critique any matching rule (range overlap or otherwise); it has no equivalence margin, no TOST, no CIs, no power or runs-needed analysis; it never treats one implementation as the reference and asks whether another is 'the same benchmark'; and it reports single point estimates with no run-to-run variance, so it cannot separate implementation differences from sampling noise. Its setting (deterministic loglik scoring of static MCQ sets) is also far from stochastic agentic benchmarks where k=3 runs per side and per-task paired results matter. The paper is useful as motivation: an independent demonstration that 'same benchmark, different implementation' shifts scores by 5-26 points, which is exactly why a port needs a real equivalence check rather than an overlap heuristic. Position against it in one sentence of related work; it does not narrow contributions (1), (2) or (3).

title: Claude 4.5+ & gpt5.4 models doing too well on Swebenchpro (Harbor issue #1067)
authors: Jason Lim (jasonlim-cerberus); thread participants: miguelrc-scale, Alex Shaw (alexgshaw), Slimshilin, Robert Zhang (robertzhidealx), justinphan3110cais, benbrandt
what_it_does: Bug report, not a statistical study. The reporter ran SWE-bench Pro through Harbor and got Opus-4.5 at 71.7% vs the official 45.89±3.60 (and Opus-4.6 at 79.6%), then root-caused it: adapter.py line 291 baked `git checkout {gold_commit} -- {test_files}` into the Dockerfile at build time, so the solution-version test files were present in the image and visible to the agent; the official base image (jefzda/sweap-images) does not contain them. Trajectory analysis across 8 models on all 731 tasks found agents read the gold test files in 56-90% of tasks. Fix merged same day as PR #1070; follow-ups #1071 (strip instance_id/commit metadata from instructions), #1083 (restore gold tests at grading time), #1159 (strip git refs; closed as out of scope because the exploit is "intrinsic to SWE-bench Pro"). The parity experiment is mentioned only as something that failed to catch the leak (comment 6, robertzhidealx: "Very strange that our prior parity experiments didn't catch it") and as a sanity check to re-run (comments 7-9). The post-fix re-validation (PR #1161, merged 2026-03-16; HF parity-experiments discussion #147) is a table of mean ± SEM: original 65.0 ± 6.5 (runs 50,60,80,70) vs Harbor 62.5 ± 2.5 (runs 60,70,60,60), codex/gpt-5.4, 10 tasks x 4 runs, labelled "confirm continued parity". The pre-fix parity row (parity_experiment.json, 2025-12-21, codex/gpt-5-mini, 100 tasks, 6 runs) was original 35.7 ± 0.6 vs Harbor 36.3 ± 1.0, i.e. ranges overlapped and the adapter passed while the leak was live. No one in the issue, the five linked PRs, the README, or the HF discussion mentions range overlap, SEM-based matching, power, confidence intervals, equivalence margins, or TOST. The only "analysis" of a gap is in PR #1083: "I analyzed the 2-task gap - it's simply codex being non-deterministic."
what_it_leaves_open: Everything our paper plans: (1) no statistical treatment of parity data at all; (2) no critique of the range-overlap rule, even though this thread is the clearest documented case of an overlap-passing adapter (35.7±0.6 vs 36.3±1.0, 6 runs each) hiding a defect that inflated a stronger model by ~26 points; (3) no equivalence test or margin; (4) the post-fix "continued parity" claim rests on 10 tasks x 4 runs with run-score ranges 50-80 vs 60-70, which cannot bound the Harbor-original difference to within a few points by any method; our CI/TOST re-analysis of this row would be a concrete, citable example. Two caveats our paper should state honestly: (a) the failure of the pre-fix parity run to detect the leak is only partly a statistical-power problem; it is also an agent/model-sensitivity problem (gpt-5-mini/codex may simply not exploit leaked tests the way Opus 4.5 does), so a stronger test on the same runs would not necessarily have flagged it; (b) the "original" side of both swebenchpro parity runs is a maintainer fork (robertzhidealx/SWE-bench_Pro-os, branch harbor-adapter), not the upstream ScaleAI harness, and whether that fork also leaked gold tests is not stated in any source read. Also quotable: the maintainers' own definition of the goal, "behaviorally equivalent to the original when evaluated on the same agent/model setup" (PR #1159 comment, 2026-03-13), which is an equivalence claim with no equivalence test behind it.

title: Coding Agents Have Converged: Why the SWE-bench Leaderboard Can No Longer Order Its Top Entries, and What to Measure Instead
date: 2026-09-15 (arXiv v1, the only version listed; camera-ready for ADMA 2026)
authors: Fengshuo Liu (Imperial College London), Ying Liu (Hong Kong Polytechnic University), Ruize Sun (Korea University), Lie Luo (Jinan University), Siyuan Guo (Jinan University)
venue: arXiv preprint 2609.17394 [cs.SE, cs.AI]; accepted at ADMA 2026 (International Conference on Advanced Data Mining and Applications), Special Session on Responsible Data Intelligence; 15 pages, 4 figures. Companion repo github.com/Adkid-Zephyr/resolution-audit (created 2026-08-01, 0 stars).
what_it_does: An observational audit of the SWE-bench leaderboard using only the per-instance verdicts the maintainers publish for 254 submissions across four splits (Verified, Lite, Test, Multimodal), with no model runs. Everything is within one harness: all entries "graded by the same official harness on the same instances" (Sec. 2). It (a) defines an effective size n_eff(S) = number of instances not solved-by-all or solved-by-none within a comparison set, showing it collapses to 0.33 for the Verified top ten and 0.07 for the top two; (b) defines a nesting coefficient against a score-implied baseline (frontier median 0.935 vs 0.774); (c) reconstructs a model x scaffold factorial from metadata and finds within-model scaffold ranges up to 29.8 pp vs an 8.8 pp top-thirty spread, with 6 of 9 interaction tests Holm-significant via paired bootstrap over instances; (d) applies exact paired McNemar tests to adjacent pairs in the top thirty: 0 of 29 separable on Verified and Lite, 14 of 23 on the 2,294-instance Test split; (e) builds descriptive tiers from a leader-based linkage rule (3 tiers uncorrected, 2 after Holm) while stressing non-rejection is not equivalence; (f) gives a discordant-instance budget formula |b-c| >~ 1.96 sqrt(b+c), k >= 1.96^2 (b+c)/(b-c)^2 (Eq. 3, Sec. 6.1) to price how many new instances a comparison would need (median 52x, ~26,000 instances for the top adjacent pairs); (g) releases a five-step 'resolution audit' protocol (profile n_eff, nesting, paired McNemar with Holm, tier partition, budget). Design implications (Sec. 6) are about SWE-bench governance (report n_eff, record model/scaffold/version, publish tiers, fix the missing-verdict convention) and internal model-selection suites. Keyword search of the full text: 0 hits for harbor, parity, port, adapter, terminal-bench, TOST, reimplement, SEM, confidence interval, k=3; 'overlap' appears only as 'Verified overlap' (split overlap), set-overlap in the nesting definition, and 'pretraining overlap'. The companion README also has 0 hits for harbor/parity/adapter/TOST/equivalence. The full text runs to 5,889 words.
what_it_leaves_open: Everything our paper does. (1) It never looks at a port, a re-implementation, a second harness, or Harbor; its own Limitations say "The pool is one benchmark family, one harness, and voluntarily submitted" and the cross-harness question is deferred ("A controlled factorial running the same scaffolds over the same models under one harness would be decisive and is future work"). (2) It explicitly declines equivalence testing: "Non-rejection does not establish equivalence or non-inferiority: we specify no practical equivalence margin" (Sec. 5), and repeats five more times that tiers "do not establish equivalence". Our TOST-with-stated-margin on Harbor parity data fills precisely the gap it names. (3) It has one run per submission and cannot speak to run-to-run noise: "Between-system differences cannot be separated from run-to-run variance... they omit execution variability" (Sec. 7); its only repeat-run datum is a crude 'replication floor' from five repeat submissions (ranges 13/15/27/41/116 instances, median 5.4 pp, Sec. 4.1). Our k=3-per-side SEM/CI analysis and the false-alarm/miss rates of the range-overlap rule are untouched. (4) It never evaluates any matching/acceptance criterion like Harbor's range overlap. What we should reuse and position against: its exact paired McNemar on per-instance verdicts (Sec. 5, Protocol 1 step 3) is the same primitive as our paired per-task parity analysis, and its Eq. 3 discordant budget can be inverted for parity (how many tasks/runs needed to exclude a gap of delta); its 'non-rejection is not equivalence' warning is exactly the inferential error the Harbor overlap rule commits, so we can cite it as naming the error in the leaderboard setting while we are the first to apply the remedy (TOST) to ports. Its Sec. 6.2 item 1 ("evaluate (M, your harness) rather than transferring an external model ranking") and item 5 (pre-register the missing/timeout verdict convention) support our motivation that scores are harness-dependent, but it measures none of that. Two further leads it cites were screened separately at abstract level (see their rows in phase1_candidates.csv): Kotawala 2026, "Resolution diagnostics for paired LLM evaluation", arXiv 2605.30315 (the origin of its paired adjacent-rank testing and sample-size inversion; found unresolvable pairs on other leaderboards, 11 of 40 and 4 of 9), and Neuhof & Benjamini 2026, "Rank intervals for leaderboards", arXiv 2606.08679. Both look like neighbors, not port/parity work, but they are the closest statistical kin to our contribution (3).

title: PaperBench Adapter: parity-validated integration (Harbor PR #408)

Its only treatment of ports/parity is one paragraph and one figure caption in Appendix D ("Adapters"): it says 26 external benchmarks were adapted into the Harbor task format and that each adapter was "validated via parity experiments", defined as "controlled comparisons where identical agents and models are evaluated on both the original and adapted versions across multiple trials", which "ensure that adaptation preserves the benchmark's evaluation semantics without introducing artifacts"; adapters are integrated "only after passing these verification tests". Statistics appear only for the main leaderboard: each agent-model pair is run "at least five times" and Figure 1 / Table 2 report resolution rates with 95% confidence intervals (method of CI not stated). Section 5 notes residual non-determinism (hardware, external APIs) and the ABC checklist self-assessment (B.5, item III.9) concedes the paper "does not provide quantitative estimates of how such flaws impact benchmark results". Reading depth: main body Sections 1-7 and Appendix D read in full, Appendix A prose, B.5 and Appendix I read; the remaining ~100 pages of appendices (judge prompts, failure taxonomies, per-task descriptions) were keyword-searched for parity/adapter/overlap/equivalence/statistics terms. Venue: arXiv preprint (cs.SE, cs.AI); citation count not checked on Semantic Scholar.
what_it_leaves_open: Everything our paper plans to do. It asserts that parity experiments "guarantee consistent and reliable evaluation" but never says what passing means, how many runs are used, or shows a single parity result, so it neither tests nor questions the matching rule. It does not analyse parity_experiment.json data, does not compute CIs or equivalence tests on original-vs-port scores, does not do per-task paired analysis, and does not ask how many runs would be needed to establish equivalence within a stated margin. The contrast is itself useful for us: the same authors report 95% CIs from >=5 runs for the leaderboard yet offer only an unquantified "parity" assurance for the 26 ports. The paper is a primary-source citation for (a) the adapter/parity concept and its claimed guarantee and (b) the maintainers' own acknowledgement of run-to-run non-determinism, not competing work.

title: What Does an Evaluation License? A Commit-Bound Census of Claim Replay in Inspect Evals
authors: Xi Qin, Jizhou Tong (Wuhan University)
venue: arXiv preprint, cs.SE (cs.AI), 36 pages with reproduction package in source archive; no publication venue found (not checked on Semantic Scholar, so unconfirmed)
what_it_does: Read in full (HTML v4, main text + Appendices A-L). The paper freezes Inspect Evals at commit 32b79a2 (124 eligible units) and asks whether each unit's historical/published claim (score, winner, full ranking, pairwise relations) can be "replayed" from bound evidence (frozen outputs, judge traces, support masks). 110 units "stop" for lack of bound evidence; 14 permit deterministic analysis. For those, it enumerates an admitted family of evaluator specifications (aggregation rule, eligibility, missingness/DNF handling, metric cutoff) and computes "claim-relative identified sets": does the winner/order/pair stay fixed across evaluator meanings? Its subject is semantic multiplicity and evidence preservation, not run-to-run noise or port fidelity. Full-text term counts: "Harbor" 0, "parity" 0, "Terminal-Bench" 0, "overlap" 0, "TOST" 0, "standard error" 0, "confidence interval" 1 (only to say sampling variation is a separate coordinate it does not analyse). "equivalence" appears 7 times, all meaning judge reference-equivalence or the Multicurious citation, never statistical equivalence. The closest it gets to a port-vs-original comparison is three deterministic audits on rounded published tables: App. E.2 BBEH ("inspect_reproduction" vs "original_paper" GPT-4o over 23 tasks: sample-micro 0.2150 vs 0.2230, task-macro 0.2209 vs 0.2281, harmonic 0.0790 vs 0.0605 -> winner non-identified across aggregation rules), App. E.3 Personality (which reproduction profile is closest to its paper reference under MAE/RMSE/Pearson), and App. H AIR Bench ("tested-versus-paper direction stays positive"). App. E.1 TheAgentCompany compares inspect_haiku45 vs original_sonnet4 (different models, so not a parity comparison). None of these uses a CI, SEM, hypothesis or equivalence test, margin, or repeated runs; they ask only whether ordering flips under different aggregation formulas. Bootstrap CIs appear only in Appendix L on an unrelated non-Inspect substrate (AgentRx/TELBench). Ancillary package listing (arxiv.org/src/2608.19269v4/anc) is Inspect-only, no Harbor/parity files.
what_it_leaves_open: Everything our paper plans: (1) it never examines the power or false-alarm rate of any port-matching criterion, and never mentions range overlap or k=3 run designs; (2) it does not touch Harbor, Terminal-Bench, parity_experiment.json, or the HF parity-experiments dataset; (3) it explicitly brackets sampling uncertainty as a separate coordinate ("a bootstrap or confidence interval varies observations under one fixed f") and disclaims any "independent-replication" claim (App. A.3 Table 6), so it offers no CIs, SEM, TOST, equivalence margins, or paired per-task analysis of original-vs-port scores; (4) its reproduction-vs-original comparisons (BBEH, Personality, AIR Bench) are deterministic ordering checks over rounded published tables under alternative aggregation rules, not statistical parity tests. It is complementary: it argues a port can be runnable yet fail to preserve enough evidence to reconstruct the original claim (semantic/provenance axis), whereas we argue a port can pass Harbor's check yet not be shown equivalent in score (sampling/statistical axis). Worth one sentence in related work as the nearest "is the ported eval still licensing the original claim?" study for Inspect Evals, and its BBEH inspect_reproduction-vs-original_paper table is a concrete example of a port comparison made without any statistical test. The authors' companion preprint "Observability is not specification: specification sensitivity and implementation stability in agent diagnosis" (Qin & Tong 2026, Zenodo, cited in Sec. 6.3) was not opened; its title mentions implementation stability, so it is a possible further neighbor.

title: When Top-k Truncation Is Not the Bottleneck: An Equivalence-Test Audit of LLM Logprob Calibration
date: 2026-07-11 (ICML 2026 Hypothesis Testing Workshop poster, Seoul); predecessor preprint "Calibration Under API Logprob Truncation: Evidence from Multiple-Choice QA" dated April 2026 (repo commit 2026-04-10)
authors: Robert (Robby) Sneiderman, sole author, independent researcher (Canada; GitHub Robby955)
what_it_does: A single-author methods-plus-case-study paper arguing that equivalence claims in LLM evaluation must be made with equivalence tests (TOST) at a pre-specified margin with paired-bootstrap inference, not with non-significant NHST results. The object of study is API logprob top-k truncation in forced 4-choice MCQA: it artificially truncates full-vocabulary vLLM logprobs at k=5 vs full and shows ΔECE ≈ 0 with TOST equivalence at margin 0.02 ECE (p_TOST < 0.001, four model/benchmark conditions). It also runs TOST on two other "measurement channel" comparisons: the same model (Qwen3-235B) served via Together AI vs self-hosted vLLM on GPQA Diamond (ΔECE = −0.015, 95% CI [−0.090, 0.058], p_TOST = 0.44, verdict "Not equiv.") and FP16 vs FP8 quantization, both inconclusive at the 0.02 margin because of wide CIs; it reports a power table (7% power at n=167 and Δ=0.02) and is explicit that equivalence was confirmed only because the observed delta was exactly zero. The ICML (July 2026) version adds an "analytical leg", a pre-registered K=3 benchmark of channel pairs on GPQA Diamond at a Brier margin of 0.015 (all three inconclusive at n=198), and a deviation log. There is no mention anywhere of Harbor, Terminal-Bench, adapters, benchmark ports, harness re-implementations, parity experiments, or any range-overlap criterion (search of the full preprint LaTeX: 0 hits for harbor/parity/adapter/port/harness/re-implement; the only repo-wide "Harbor"/"parity" hits are question-bank text, "The Harbor Lights Boat Company" and "intrinsic parity -1"). The author's CV calls this the "first of three venues on this question" (also UAI 2026 Safe AI workshop and Sci-FM 2026) and lists a sibling paper "Measurement-Channel Mismatch in Production LLM Pipelines" (UK AI Conference 2026, OpenReview, not retrievable) on the same measurement-channel theme; none mention Harbor or ports. His only Harbor-adjacent activity is a pure fork of harbor-framework/terminal-bench-science (0 commits ahead) and five task-submission PRs there, none about parity. Read-depth caveat: the ICML version is available only on OpenReview (mRzfHyrPvS), which could not be retrieved; there is no Wayback Machine snapshot, testing.ml links only to OpenReview, and the ICML poster-media page was not available. The ICML abstract was therefore read in full (icml.cc page), together with the complete LaTeX of the April 2026 predecessor from github.com/Robby955/logprobe-calibration (paper/main.tex, 1308 lines, same experiments and numbers: CalProbe-167, TOST at 0.02 ECE, aggregator spread 0.15-0.29), plus its equivalence-test script and result tables.
what_it_leaves_open: Everything specific to our paper: it never looks at Harbor, its adapters, parity_experiment.json, or the HF parity-experiments dataset; it never discusses or critiques a range-overlap (min/max) matching rule or any k=3-runs-per-side protocol; it never compares a re-implemented/ported benchmark against its original harness; it has no per-task paired analysis across two harnesses; and it gives no run-count/margin recommendations for agentic benchmark scores (its units are MCQA items and ECE/Brier, n=167-500 items, not k=3 whole-benchmark runs). What it does pre-empt is purely methodological: the "state a margin in advance, use TOST with paired bootstrap, report inconclusive honestly, show the power table" framing for LLM-evaluation equivalence claims already exists in a 2026 ICML workshop paper (and two sibling venues), and its Together-vs-vLLM "same model, different serving channel" comparison is a close analogue of "same agent, different harness". Our contribution (3) should therefore be positioned as applying/adapting an equivalence-test protocol of this kind to harness parity (with benchmark-run-level units, per-task pairing, and a Harbor-specific margin), not as introducing TOST-with-margin to LLM evaluation. Residual risk: the July ICML full text and the UAI/Sci-FM/UK-AI-Conference versions were not read; the ICML abstract's "channel pairs" and "rest of the pipeline" refer to logprob-pipeline channels (temperature swap, provider, aggregator), so a hidden harness-port section is unlikely but not excluded.
